    Clifford Algebra

    Clifford algebra is a way to encode an inner-product space into an associative algebra so that vectors multiply according to the metric.

    Let \((V,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a real inner-product space. The real Clifford algebra \(\mathrm{Cl}(V)\) is the associative algebra generated by \(V\) subject to the relation

    \[ v\cdot v=-|v|^2\,1, \qquad v\in V. \]

    Equivalently, by polarization,

    \[ \boxed{ v\cdot w+w\cdot v = -2\langle v,w\rangle\,1. } \]

    Thus orthogonal vectors anticommute:

    \[ v\perp w \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v\cdot w=-w\cdot v, \]

    while a unit vector satisfies

    \[ v^2=-1. \]

    Remark
    Edit

    A formal definition uses the tensor algebra. Start with

    \[ T(V) = \mathbb R \oplus V \oplus (V\otimes V) \oplus (V^{\otimes3}) \oplus\cdots . \]

    Then quotient out by the ideal generated by

    \[ v\otimes v+|v|^2 1. \]

    Thus

    \[ \boxed{ \Cl(V) = T(V)\Big/ \left\langle v\otimes v+|v|^2 1 :\ v\in V \right\rangle . } \]

    In practice, you rarely need the quotient construction explicitly. The useful rule is simply

    \[ v\cdot w+w\cdot v = -2\langle v,w\rangle. \]

    For example, if \(\{e_1,\dots,e_m\}\) is an orthonormal basis of \(V\), then

    \[ e_i^2=-1, \qquad e_ie_j=-e_je_i \quad (i\neq j). \]

    As a vector space,

    \[ \Cl(V) \]

    is spanned by

    \[ 1,\quad e_i,\quad e_ie_j,\quad e_ie_je_k,\quad\ldots \]

    with strictly increasing indices. Hence

    \[ \dim \Cl(V)=2^m. \]

    Proposition
    Edit

    Given a real vector space \(V\) and a quadratic form \(q\), the Clifford algebra \(\mathrm{Cl}(V,q)\) is defined unique up to canonical algebra isomorphism because of its universal property.
